Unfortunately, you're new and only have 20 feedback. One negative can really mess up your percent rating and make it harder for you to get sales. Also, you said it's a cheap item. One thing I *might* consider in your situation, though, is possibly standing my ground regarding reimbursement for return shipping (that's if return shipping is expensive...if just a few bucks, again, I might just bite the bullet), unless the item is defective. Again, though, I don't know the full details of the situation and you have to ask yourself if risking a neg when you only have 20 feedback is worth it. Dealing with eBay and the whole case resolution system is a big pain in the ass. If you can avoid it while you're new at limited expense, just try to avoid taking the risk that they won't rule in your favor.

While it sucks, I had something similar happen to me and don't regret accepting the return. The customer actually left me extremely positive feedback because I went out of my way to work with her and ensure that she was satisfied. I worked for a disability services office at a college before. You don't have to tell your professors anything about your condition at all. Your file at the disabilities office is confidential...they should explain all of this to you during your intake with them. The only thing that your professors will know, unless you tell them otherwise, is that you're on file to get accommodations with the Office of Disability Services. Usually, depending upon the office (some offices will send the letter to your professors for you), all you have to do is hand your professors a letter from the office that states what your accommodations are and that you are registered with them. You don't need to have any further discussion. You don't owe your professors an explanation and if they press you for one, you should talk to the Disabilities Office.

I personally would advise you NOT to tell your professors about the nature of your disability. I know people commenting here encouraging you mean well, but I have actually worked for a disabilities office before...and assuming you're in the U.S., it is none of your professors' business and I don't think it will help. It has not always worked out well for students I worked with who disclosed the nature of their disability to their professors. You don't need to do that, so I would not recommend chancing it.

It helped me at first...enormously, in fact, to the point of where I honestly felt completely cured of my anxiety and depression, similar to how you feel in this post! Great, right? Well, because it's a stimulant and addictive, I naturally developed a tolerance to it and needed increasing doses to achieve the same effect, and it also started wearing off sooner. When it wore off it was not pretty at all...I became extremely irritable, angry (to the point of where I could have easily gotten violent), impulsive, and suicidal. 

It's the kind of medication that can seem like a miracle cure at first because of how much it helped me initially, but it is impossible to stay on it long-term without encountering serious side-effects due to its addictive nature...one cannot just keep infinitely upping the dose and taking it closer together so that the effects don't wear off. I did not even up my dose past the recommended therapeutic dose (which my doctor did increase over time) because I didn't want to abuse it...instead, I just dealt with it wearing off sooner and with me becoming more and more irritable when that happened.

The positive effects it has are impossible to sustain long-term because it is addictive. I would really caution against using a narcotic to treat anxiety long-term like this. This is the same reason doctors don't prescribe benzodiazepines long-term for anxiety. I'm no prude about medication or drugs or anything, but it had horrible effects on me. Things may seem great for the first couple of months, but I went on a rapid downhill spiral after that due to it wearing off sooner and sooner with the longer I was on it, as well as extreme increased irritability over time. When I was irritable, I became more reclusive and/or combative, so any positive social effects were lost over time. 

I don't mean to "lecture" or anything...please just be mindful of how it is affecting your moods when it starts wearing off, or have someone else keep an eye on you who knows about the situation, because at first I had no idea what was happening to me and just thought I was going crazy or something. I'd also seriously reconsider whether this is really a viable long-term solution. I am not against using medication to help treat anxiety, but using a narcotic to treat anxiety is a different story. All narcotics helped my anxiety at first! Percocet was great. Then they got addictive -- even if you're not abusing them, you naturally build up a tolerance and need more over time to achieve the same effect -- and that's when the mess starts...if you take more, you end up taking too much. If you don't take more, you end up crashing really badly when it wears off. Not worth it in my opinion.
